column13: A steady compounder: sales and profit grow at a double-digit pace, returns on capital stay high and borrowing is low. Use it to see how a long record shows up in 5-year averages and CAGRs.
A cyclical business: sales and margins rise and fall with an industry cycle. Its P/E looks lowest when profits are at a peak, which is why one-year ratios can mislead for such companies.
Cash-rich and debt-free: there are no borrowings and no finance cost, so interest coverage is not meaningful. Much of its other income is interest on surplus cash.
A leveraged utility: heavy fixed assets funded largely with debt. Debt to equity is high and interest coverage is thin, which is common for power businesses but still worth understanding.
A possible value trap: the P/E is low, but sales are shrinking and margins are slipping. A low multiple on falling earnings can stay low.
A turnaround: several loss-making years followed by a return to profit. Growth rates across the change from loss to profit are not meaningful and are marked as turnarounds.
A fast grower with a rich valuation: sales grow quickly and the P/E is very high. Compare its growth with its valuation before drawing conclusions.
A red-flag teaching case: debtor days have risen sharply in recent years while sales growth stayed slow, so more of the reported sales are still waiting to be collected.
A loss-maker: operating losses every year, funded by fresh equity and borrowings. P/E is not meaningful, so its reference price is set on sales.

A typical company for its sector with no special pattern. It is here so that its peer group has enough members for medians and percentiles. Listed recently: only four financial years of statements are available, so 5-year and 10-year figures show 'not enough history'.
A well-run lender: steady loan growth, few bad loans and healthy returns on assets. Lender metrics such as NIM, GNPA and credit cost apply; ROCE and debt to equity do not.

An insurer with minimal fields only. There are just four insurers in the sample, fewer than the five needed for peer statistics, so percentiles show 'too few comparable companies'. Its company type is left blank on purpose, so the app infers it from the sector name.
